messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 21
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Bus Driver
  trauma_type: Military
  pcl5: 53

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Screen Escape: I spend long hours on my phone, games, or internet to avoid thinking, Avoid Religious Spaces: Places of worship or religious gatherings, Avoid Crowds: Crowded places such as shopping centres or public events
  Memory: Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
  Negative Appraisals: Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time
  Triggers: Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell, Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds, Auditory (Helicopter): Helicopter or aircraft sounds

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Liam Weber was 21 when he came for treatment, a quiet young man who had returned from military service carrying an experience he still could not tell straight through. During a convoy operation overseas, an explosion struck near his vehicle. What remained with him was not a single coherent story but flashes: the blast, the metallic pressure in his ears, a smear of smoke, shouted words he could not piece back together, and above all the scorched, burnt smell that seemed to fuse itself to the moment. He also remembered the chopping aircraft noise overhead afterward, and the way every sudden bang became charged with the expectation that something catastrophic was about to happen again. When he tried to explain what happened, he would stop, frown, and say he knew it had happened but could not find the words for it.

In the months after returning home, Liam had come to believe that the world was fundamentally dangerous and that his only chance of getting through a day was to stay on guard. He scanned sounds automatically, especially any sharp bang or the distant thrum of a helicopter or plane, and his body reacted before he had time to think. That sense of permanent threat narrowed his life. Although he now worked as a bus driver, he approached each route as if danger might break into it without warning. At crowded stops he watched passengers, exits, and sudden movements instead of settling into the routine of the job. He had also begun avoiding crowded places outside work altogether, turning down invitations to shopping centers or public events because being surrounded by people felt unsafe in a way he could not easily justify to others.

Those beliefs also shaped what he did when he was alone. Because he was certain that letting his mind go quiet would leave him exposed to whatever came back, he spent long hours on his phone, gaming, or scrolling online late into the night, trying to keep himself mentally occupied. He had stopped going into churches or other religious spaces as well; he would detour past them without fully explaining why, only knowing they left him too exposed and unsettled. Beneath that was a more despairing conviction he rarely said aloud: that he was no longer sure his life was worth living. He did not describe an active plan, but the thought frightened him because it arrived with the same flat certainty as his other conclusions about the world.

The memories themselves fed those conclusions. Because the event returned in disconnected pieces, Liam could not place it safely in the past. Instead it replayed like a film that started without warning: a burst of noise, the smell of burning, the aircraft sound overhead, and then a sickening sense that he was back in it. Each replay seemed to confirm what he already feared—that nowhere was truly safe and that he had to remain vigilant at all times. What frightened him most was not only remembering but the fact that the memory felt unfinished and beyond his control, as if his mind were still trying and failing to make sense of something too dangerous to hold.

That was part of why he kept reaching for distraction. When a memory began to gather, he would grab his phone, start a game, or disappear into the internet for hours because it was the fastest way he knew to stop the images from gaining momentum. Avoiding crowds helped for the same reason: fewer noises, fewer jolts, fewer chances of a bang setting off the internal replay. Yet over time this left the memory even less spoken and less organized. The more he pushed it away and replaced quiet moments with screens, the more the event seemed to survive only as broken clips and sensory fragments, still impossible to describe from beginning to end.

Nowhere was this clearer than at work. If a bus backfired nearby, if a passenger dropped something with a sharp crack, or if diesel exhaust carried a burnt smell through the cab, Liam could feel the film begin again. He would tighten at the wheel, lose the thread of the present, and afterward spend his break staring at his phone to force the images down. Even the sound of helicopters over the city could alter the rest of his shift. He hated how quickly this happened, and each episode left him more convinced that the danger was real, current, and inescapable.

By the time he sought help, Liam’s world had become smaller and more exhausting than he wanted to admit. He was still showing up to work, but much of his life outside those routes had collapsed into avoidance and screen time. What finally brought him in was the realization that he could no longer tell whether he was protecting himself or disappearing from his own life. He said he wanted, more than anything, to be able to remember what happened without feeling trapped inside it, and he was afraid that if nothing changed, the part of him that still cared whether his life was worth living would go quiet for good.
